messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Aroha

Aroha was thirty-one when she first came to therapy, though the weight she carried made her seem older in the studio. She had grown up in Auckland, the middle child of three, watching her father's hands become weapons in the kitchen while her mother stood frozen at the counter. The violence wasn't constant—there were long stretches of ordinary Tuesday mornings—but it was always possible, lurking beneath the surface of her father's silences. His name was David. She hadn't heard it spoken aloud in years, but when someone in the dance company mentioned their brother David, or when she glimpsed the name on a cast list, her chest would tighten and her heart would begin to race without warning, as though her body remembered something her mind was trying to forget.

She had moved to Los Angeles at twenty-two to dance professionally, and for a time, the distance and the work had felt like salvation. The stage gave her a place to channel the restlessness that had lived in her since childhood. But marriage to James, a kind and steady man, had brought a different kind of vulnerability. Five years in, she found herself hyperaware of his moods—the way he set down a glass, the particular silence that fell between them on Sunday mornings. She wasn't afraid of him; she was afraid of herself, of some essential flaw that had made her father's rage inevitable and that might, in ways she couldn't articulate, make her deserving of it. When she recalled the specific moments—her father's face above her mother's, the sound of breaking dishes—she felt a crushing shame, as though she had witnessed something obscene and her witnessing had somehow made her complicit. At other times, she could summon the images with perfect clarity but feel nothing at all, as though she were watching a film about someone else's life, which was, in its own way, more terrifying.

The triggers multiplied. Being watched—truly observed—became intolerable. During rehearsals, when the choreographer moved through the studio offering corrections, Aroha's breath would shallow. The feeling of being seen, assessed, scrutinized, sent her back to childhood moments when she had tried to be invisible, when her smallness might keep her safe. And because she had come to believe, deep in the part of her that still felt like a frightened child, that there was something fundamentally wrong with her—something that invited violation—being watched felt like exposure. That belief then shaped what she noticed: a colleague's glance held too long became proof that people were not what they seemed, that beneath every kind word lay judgment or worse. These appraisals fed back into her triggers; the more she believed she was inherently flawed, the more any observation felt like a threat, and the more her heart would race, her body flooding with adrenaline as though danger were imminent.

The memory itself had become a kind of trap. When something—a name, a raised voice in the hallway, the particular way James touched her shoulder—brought the full memory back without warning, it arrived complete with all the shame and all the conviction of her own culpability. But sometimes she could access the memory without emotion, and that dissociation, that numbness, felt like further proof that she was broken, that normal feeling had been burned out of her long ago. These oscillations between shame and numbness, between vivid recall and disconnection, reinforced her conviction that she could not trust her own mind, which meant she could not trust anyone else's either. James had begun to notice her withdrawal, the way she flinched when he approached from behind, the nights she claimed exhaustion rather than let him close. He loved her, she knew that, but she had come to believe that his love was based on a misunderstanding of who she was—and that eventually, inevitably, he would see what she saw: that she carried something contaminated, something that made violence possible.

It was James who finally insisted she seek help. He had found her in the studio late one evening, sitting on the floor in street clothes, her heart still pounding from an ordinary rehearsal, unable to explain to him why she couldn't move, couldn't breathe, couldn't believe that the threat she felt was not real. She came to therapy because she was losing her marriage and her career, because she could no longer distinguish between memory and present danger, and because some part of her, the part that had once loved dance, was desperate to know if she could ever feel safe again.
